events.text: You stop to drink at a pool high in the mountains, the kind with no stream in and no stream out, black as an inkstone. There is no wind. And yet, every few breaths, a string of bubbles rises from the middle of it, big as fists, and breaks without a sound. That evening a single grey cloud parks itself over the pool and rains on it, and only on it, for an hour. That night you dream of a shining bead falling through the dark, turning over and over, and something enormous below it, reaching.

choices.text: Sit by the pool until dawn and watch the bubbles

effects.log: The bubbles come at the same slow rhythm all night, like breathing. Toward dawn you realise you have matched your own breath to it without meaning to. You leave the mountain with your qi deeper and a feeling you are being remembered.

choices.text: Throw a stone in to see how deep it goes

effects.log: The stone goes in without a splash. A moment later the whole surface of the pool shivers once, like the skin of a horse, and every bird on the mountain takes off at the same time. You do not throw another.

choices.text: Go down to the nearest village and ask about the pool

effects.log: An old woman shelling beans tells you the pool has a name nobody says aloud, that nobody throws stones in it, and that in her grandmother's time the rain came from it when it came from nowhere else. "Did you dream?" she asks. You say nothing. She nods as if you had.

events.text: Years later a summer storm catches you on the ridge above the black pool. Lightning, and for one white breath you see it: a serpent as long as a river barge, green-black and hornless, rearing out of the pool toward something falling through the rain, small and burning like a coal. A pearl. The jaws close on nothing. That night it speaks in your dream, in a voice like stones rolling in a river: "I missed. Now they will come for me while I am weak. Men with hooks, for what is in my belly. A year from tonight."

choices.text: Ask it, in the dream, why it is telling you

effects.log: "Because you sat by my water and listened," it says. "Or because you threw a stone in it. I forget which. It does not matter. You are the only human who has dreamed this far in a hundred years."

choices.text: Wake, and sharpen your blade

effects.log: You wake before dawn with the whetstone already in your hand. You are not sure yet what the blade is for. You suspect it is not sure either.

choices.text: Wake, and count the days to the full moon

effects.log: A year. You write the date on the wall of the inn in charcoal and stare at it all morning.

events.text: A year to the night after the dream. Six hunters come up the mountain with hooked chains, nets of iron wire and a sealed letter from a sect that wants a core. Their leader, {npc}, has a face like a boot and the calm of somebody who has done this before. In the pool, the water is low and red-brown: the serpent is still bleeding from its fall. It surfaces once, sees you on the bank, and does not sink again. It is waiting to see what you will do.

choices.text: Stand with it: pour your qi into the water and hold the bank

ok.log: You put your palms on the surface of the pool and push your qi down into the dark until your arms shake. Something huge drinks it. Then you turn and face six hunters alone on the bank, and for a long and ugly hour nobody gets past you. At dawn they carry their wounded away. Behind you, very quietly, the serpent rises an arm's length out of the water and bows its head to you, once. You will dream about that bow for the rest of your life, and, it turns out, beyond it.

fail.log: They are too many and you are not enough. A hooked chain opens your side and you go into the water. Something catches you, cold and enormous, and carries you up onto the far bank. When you wake the hunters are gone, the pool is still, and there is a single green-black scale the size of a rice bowl lying on your chest. (-30 health)

choices.text: Lead the hunters astray: tell them the beast moved to the next valley

ok.log: You sit with them at their fire and tell them, with a great deal of convincing detail, about the bubbles you saw in a pool two valleys east. They break camp at dawn. Three days later a storm sits over the black pool for a whole night, and in the morning every fish in the river below is facing upstream.

fail.log: Their leader looks at you for a long time and then laughs. "Friend of the snake," {npc} says, and has you tied to a tree. The hunt fails anyway: the pool is empty when they reach it. In the morning your ropes are wet through, and loose. (-12 health)

choices.text: Hunt it: its core would make you a legend

ok.log: You join {npc} on the bank, and when the serpent comes up out of the water, slow and wounded from its fall, yours is the blade that finds the soft place under its jaw. The core is the size of a fist and warm as a living heart. You swallow its power over a single long night. The murim will say your name for years. On the anniversary, every year, you will dream of a pool with nothing in it.

fail.log: It is wounded. It is not weak. The tail comes out of the dark and the bank simply is not there any more. Two of the hunters do not come up. You do, barely, coughing black water, and it looks at you once from the middle of the pool with an eye as big as a cartwheel before it sinks. (-35 health)

choices.text: Walk away. This is not your fight

effects.log: You take the long road down the mountain and do not look back. Behind you, that night, a storm sits on one peak all night. You never learn how it ended. In some other life, perhaps, you will.

events.text: You have never been to this mountain. You know the way up anyway. At the top is a black pool with no stream in and no stream out, and bubbles rising from its middle in a slow rhythm, and you know, the way you know your own name, that you sat beside it once in a life that ended before you found out why.

choices.text: Sit down where you sat before

effects.log: The stone is worn smooth in the shape of somebody. You fit it exactly. The bubbles stop for a long moment, as if something below has looked up.

choices.text: Call out to whatever is in the water

effects.log: "I came back," you say, feeling foolish. A ring spreads out across the pool from nowhere. That night the dream of the falling bead comes back as if it had never stopped.

events.text: A storm finds you on the ridge above the black pool, as if it had been looking. In the lightning the serpent rises: hornless, enormous, reaching for a falling pearl, and missing. In the dream that night it says: "You again. The last time, you did not stay to the end. They are coming for my core. A year from tonight. Stay this time, one way or another."

choices.text: Promise it you will stay

effects.log: "Do not promise," it says. "Be here." It is the most reasonable thing anybody has said to you in years.

choices.text: Ask it what happened, the last time

effects.log: "You died of something small," it says. "Humans do. It was very irritating." You wake laughing, which you did not expect.

events.text: The hunters come up the mountain exactly when it said they would: six of them, hooked chains, iron nets, a sect's letter. {npc} leads them, steady and unhurried. The pool is low and stained with the serpent's blood. It rises once and looks straight at you, and this time it does not look surprised.

events.text: Wading in the stream above the village for crayfish, you put your hand on something round and smooth and cold between two stones: an egg, white as a pearl, as big as a goose egg and a great deal heavier. When you hold it to your ear, something inside it is very slowly turning over.

choices.text: Take it home and keep it warm under your blanket

effects.log: It sleeps under your blanket for a whole winter, colder than you no matter how long you hold it. The grown-ups say it is a stone. You do not argue. You know better.

choices.text: Put it back exactly where it was

effects.log: You set it back between the two stones and pile pebbles round it so the current cannot take it. You visit it every few days all summer. One morning there is only an empty shell, and a thin silver line in the mud leading into the deep water.

choices.text: Try to sell it in the market

effects.log: An apothecary gives you three coppers' worth of silver for it and then, when you have gone, closes his shop for the day. You never find out why. It bothers you for years.

events.text: In spring the egg under your blanket cracks. What comes out is as long as your finger, silver, with gold eyes far too old for its face. It looks at you. You look at it. Then it bites you, very gently, as if to taste what you are.

choices.text: Carry it back to the stream where you found it

effects.log: You let it go in the deep pool under the waterfall. It swims a circle round your ankles, three times, and then it is gone. For the rest of the summer you catch more crayfish than any child in the village.

choices.text: Keep it in a water jar and feed it frogs

effects.log: It eats a frog a day and grows a finger-length a month. By autumn it does not fit in the jar. One night the jar is empty and the window is open, and you cry, and then you understand.

events.text: Grown, you come back to the village and walk up to the waterfall pool for no good reason. You sit on the bank. After a long while the water bulges, and a head comes up, silver-green and as big as a water barrel, with gold eyes far too old for its face. It looks at you. It remembers your hand.

choices.text: Hold out your hand, the way you did when you were small

effects.log: It lays its chin on your palm, very lightly, like a cat. The cold of it goes all the way up your arm and settles somewhere behind your heart, and stays there for the rest of your life, a little cool calm when things get hot.

choices.text: Back away slowly

effects.log: It watches you go without moving. You were a child the last time. It seems to understand that people change. It does not seem to hold it against you.

events.text: Every child in the village knows the rule about the deep pool below the cliff: no stones, no shouting, no swimming, no laughing at snakes. Today the miller's boy says the rule is for babies and picks up a rock the size of his head.
events.arc: No Stones in the Dragon Pool

choices.text: Grab his arm

ok.log: You hang off his arm until he drops it. He calls you a coward all the way home. That night there is a storm over the pool and nowhere else, and in the morning he does not call you anything.

fail.log: He shoves you over and throws it. The pool swallows it without a splash. That night there is a storm over the pool and nowhere else, and the miller's roof comes off. Nobody can prove anything. Everybody knows. (-5 health)

choices.text: Run and tell his grandmother

effects.log: She comes down the path faster than any old woman should be able to, and the boy learns several new words and the reason for the rule, at length.

choices.text: Throw one too. Rules are for babies

effects.log: Both stones go in. The pool does not ripple. For three days afterwards it rains on your house and only your house, and the old women of the village look at you in a way you will remember when you are old yourself.

events.text: Years later you are passing the old village when a summer drought cracks the fields open. The headman has decided the dragon pool is angry, and the village has decided whose fault it is: the child who threw a stone in it once. You.
events.arc: No Stones in the Dragon Pool

choices.text: Go down to the pool and apologise, properly, in front of them all

effects.log: You kneel on the bank and say sorry to the water like a fool, with the whole village watching. It rains the next morning. It would have rained anyway, probably. Nobody in the village believes that, and neither, quite, do you.

choices.text: Tell them a stone thrown by a child does not stop the rain

effects.log: You are right, and nobody wants to hear it. You leave the village with half the old women spitting after you. It rains three days later.

events.text: The rice is dying in the fields. The village has hired a mudang, a shaman, to dance for the dragon of the pool. {npc} arrives with a drummer, a box of bells and an expression that says {he} has done this in worse places. {He} looks the village over and points at you. "That one carries the offering. The dragon likes a face it has not seen."

choices.text: Carry the offering down to the water

effects.log: A tray of rice cakes, a jar of clear spirit and a pig's head with a coin in its mouth, all of it down a steep path in front of the whole village. {npc} dances on the bank for half a day, and when you look back at the pool the rice cakes are gone, and you did not see them go.

choices.text: Refuse: you do not believe in any of this

effects.log: {npc} shrugs. "The dragon does not mind," {he} says. "It has been not believed in by better people than you." Somebody else carries the tray.

choices.text: Ask {npc}, quietly, whether there really is a dragon

effects.log: "There is something," {npc} says. "It is not a dragon yet. That is why it listens. Dragons do not need us. Things that are trying to be dragons do."

events.text: Three days after the rite, nothing. The headman wants the silver back from {npc}. On the fourth day a cloud comes over the hill: one cloud, small and very dark, and it stops over the pool and stays there.

choices.text: Stand with {npc} on the bank and wait

effects.log: It rains for a day and a night, on the pool first and then outward, field by field, as if somebody were walking the boundaries and watering them. {npc} does not say anything. {He} just counts the silver twice and gives half of it to you.

choices.text: Go and look into the pool while everyone else watches the sky

ok.log: For one breath, under the black water, you see an eye as big as a temple bell, gold, half-closed, patient. Then the rain starts and the surface breaks into a thousand rings.

fail.log: You see your own face, and a lot of rain. Still, you were the only one looking down.

events.text: {npc} is very old now and has sent for you. {He} is sitting up in bed in a house hung with bells. "I am going," {he} says. "Somebody has to take the pool. Not the dancing. Just the listening. It knows your face."

choices.text: Take it: promise to visit the pool once a year

effects.npcPass: old age, in the house of bells
effects.log: {npc} presses a little brass bell into your hand and dies before the summer. Every year after that you go up to the pool and sit, and ring the bell once, and every year the water answers with a ring of its own.

choices.text: Gently refuse

effects.npcPass: old age, in the house of bells
effects.log: "Fair," {npc} says. "It will find somebody. It always does." {He} dies before the summer, and the pool takes a long time to rain again.

events.text: The ferryman at the river crossing will not take you over tonight. Not for silver, not for anything. "Night of the dark moon," he says. "The Ishimi is moving. You can hear it under the boat. Come back at dawn."

choices.text: Wait for dawn like a sensible person

effects.log: You sleep in his shed. In the middle of the night the whole river makes a sound like a long breath let out, and the ferry boat rocks at its rope as if something wide had passed underneath. In the morning he takes you over and will not take your money.

choices.text: Take the boat yourself and cross

ok.log: Halfway over the boat lifts, slowly, a hand's width out of the water, and sets down again. You row the rest of the way faster than you have ever done anything.

fail.log: Halfway over the boat lifts and does not set down. You swim the rest, in the dark, with something going past you in the water for a very long time.
fail.deathCause: the river on a dark-moon night, against the ferryman's advice

choices.text: Sit with him by the fire and ask about the Ishimi

effects.log: "Older than my grandfather's grandfather," he says. "Long as three boats. Never hurt anybody who waited for dawn." He pours you hot barley tea and tells river stories until the fog lifts.

events.text: The ferryman's son keeps the crossing now. He laughs at his father's dark-moon rule and rows any hour, for double fare. Tonight is the dark moon and he is pushing off with a boat full of merchants.

choices.text: Stop him at the landing

ok.log: You tell him his father's stories in his father's words, and halfway through he stops laughing. They wait for dawn. At midnight the river breathes out, long and slow, and the son goes very pale.

fail.log: He pushes off. You stand on the landing and listen. Halfway across, the boat lifts, and comes down, and somebody screams, and then, impossibly, they are rowing again. They make it. Nobody rows on the dark moon again.

choices.text: Go with them, sword ready

effects.log: Halfway over the boat lifts. You stand in the bow with your sword out, which is useless, and stare down into the water at an eye as big as a millstone, which stares back. Then it sinks and the boat comes down. Nobody speaks until the far bank. (-8 health)

events.text: After the spring floods the whole village goes down to the river to stare at what is hanging in the willows: a shed skin, papery and silver, every scale as big as your palm, stretching along the bank for the length of four houses. Nothing that wore it is anywhere to be seen.

choices.text: Cut a piece and sell it to the apothecary

effects.log: He pays forty taels without bargaining, which tells you exactly how much he will sell it for. Within a month half the province is buying serpent-skin powder for joint pain.

choices.text: Keep a single scale for luck

effects.log: You thread it on a cord. It is cool against your skin even in summer. Years later, in a fight you should have lost, a blade skids off your chest where it hangs.

choices.text: Tell everyone to leave it alone: whatever shed it may want it back

effects.log: Nobody listens. But the next night the skin is gone from the willows, all of it at once, and nobody admits to having taken it.

events.text: Another skin in the willows, years later: longer this time, the length of eight houses, and darker. On the underside of the throat, where the scales are smallest, there is one scale lying the wrong way, against all the others.

choices.text: Study the reversed scale

effects.log: The reverse scale: the one every serpent-hunting manual describes and nobody has ever seen. You sketch it twice from every side. You understand, suddenly, why the old stories say touching it is the last mistake anyone makes.

choices.text: Leave the skin, and the scale, where they are

effects.log: Some things should not be studied by people who might one day want to use what they learned. You walk away and feel lighter for it.

events.text: A ragged child grabs your sleeve in the night market and opens a fist: a marble, cloudy and pale, that glows faintly in the dark of a cupped hand. "Dragon pearl," the child whispers. "Yeouiju. Grants wishes. Five taels."
events.arc: The Pearl in the Night Market

choices.text: Pay five taels

effects.log: It is a marble dusted with something that glows. You know that. You keep it anyway. It does not grant wishes. It does make you smile, every time you find it in your pocket, for years.

choices.text: Buy the child a meal instead

effects.log: Over a bowl of noodles the child confesses: the glow is crushed firefly and pine resin. "But the old man who taught me said the real ones glow just like that," the child adds, "only you can't look at them straight."

choices.text: Laugh and walk on

effects.log: You hear the child at the next stall: "Dragon pearl. Grants wishes. Three taels." Prices are falling.

events.text: The pale marble you bought in a night market years ago is glowing in the dark of your pocket tonight, properly, for the first time, and outside a storm is crossing the mountains in a line, as if following something.
events.arc: The Pearl in the Night Market

choices.text: Go out and hold it up to the storm

effects.log: Just firefly and resin, surely. And yet. For the length of one lightning flash something vast in the cloud turns its head toward your little light, considers it, and goes on. The marble never glows again.

choices.text: Put it under a bowl and go back to sleep

effects.log: In the morning there are claw marks in the mud of the yard, four toes wide, and the bowl is overturned. The marble is still there. Whatever it was, it was not interested in fakes.

events.text: The whole village is in the square: the fishermen have caught the Imugi of the river. It hangs from a pole between two men, black, slimy, as long as a door is tall, mouth open. It is, unmistakably, an eel.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let them have their day

effects.log: They roast it, the whole village eats it, and the headman makes a speech. It is the best eel you have ever had. Nobody mentions that the river still has bubbles in it.

choices.text: Point out that it is an eel

effects.log: "An Imugi," the headman says, very slowly, "is what we say it is." The crowd agrees. You are not offered any eel.

choices.text: Buy the head as a trophy, for a laugh

effects.log: Two taels. You nail it over the door of your room. Strangely, for years, no serpent of any size comes near your house, as if word had got round.

events.text: The next summer, a new problem: the fishermen's nets keep coming up torn from the inside, every one of them, in perfectly straight lines, as if cut. The village is no longer celebrating.

choices.text: Watch the river by night

ok.log: At midnight the river lights up from below, briefly, green, and a shape longer than the bridge passes under it without a ripple. The nets were in its way. You tell the fishermen to set them in the shallows from now on. They grumble. It works.

fail.log: You fall asleep on the bank and wake up soaked to the waist with the tide mark of a wave that should not exist on a river. (-6 health)

choices.text: Suggest the village leave an eel in the river, as an apology

effects.log: They throw a live eel back in, solemnly, with a speech. The nets come up whole after that. The headman claims this was his idea.

events.text: You are lodging with a farming family when you find a black snake as thick as your arm coiled in the rafters of their storehouse. You reach for your blade. The grandmother catches your wrist with a grip like a blacksmith's. "That," she says, "is our luck. That is the Eopgureongi. If it leaves, this house falls."

choices.text: Bow to the snake, as the family does

effects.log: You bow. The snake looks at you, decides you are furniture, and goes back to sleep. The grandmother approves of you for the rest of your stay and feeds you twice as much as before.

choices.text: Ask why a snake would bring luck

effects.log: "It eats the rats," the grandmother says, "and it keeps away worse things than rats. And when a house is cruel, it leaves, and then the house burns, or floods, or the sons gamble it away. It is not luck. It is a witness."

choices.text: Laugh: it is just a rat snake

effects.log: Nobody laughs with you. That night something drops from the rafters onto your bedroll, very heavily, and leaves again. The family say nothing at breakfast.

events.text: You pass the farm again, years later. The grandmother is dead. Her grandson is master of the house now, and he has set a rat-catcher on the storehouse with smoke and a pitchfork. "Old women's nonsense," he says.

choices.text: Stop the rat-catcher

ok.log: You tell the grandson what his grandmother told you, word for word. He goes quiet and sends the rat-catcher home. When you leave, the snake is in the rafters, watching you go.

fail.log: He has the smoke lit anyway. The snake leaves by the roof in front of everybody, slow and unhurried, and goes up the hill. That autumn the storehouse burns. Nobody is hurt. Nothing is saved.

choices.text: Carry the snake up the hill yourself, before it is killed

effects.log: It lets you lift it, heavy as a wet rope of iron, and you set it down in an old shrine on the hill. A year later you hear the shrine-keeper's family have done remarkably well.

events.text: In the martial market at the crossroads a hunter in a bearskin has drawn a crowd. On red silk in front of {him} sits a sphere of green light the size of a plum, pulsing gently. "The core of an Imugi," {npc} announces. "Three hundred years of qi in one swallow. I took it from the beast with my own hands. Eight hundred taels."

choices.text: Look closer at the core

ok.log: There is no qi in it at all. It is a ball of green glass with a fish-oil lamp hidden in the silk underneath, and a very nicely painted story. You catch {npc}'s eye. {He} catches yours. Neither of you says anything, yet.

fail.log: It pulses. It glows. It certainly looks like three hundred years of something. You come away with a headache and no certainty either way.

choices.text: Expose {npc} in front of the crowd

ok.log: You flip the silk and show the lamp. The crowd roars. {npc} runs, bearskin flapping, and the glass core rolls under a noodle stall and is never seen again.

fail.log: You flip the silk and there is nothing under it but silk. {npc} has quick hands. The crowd decides you are a jealous rival and pelts you with persimmons. (-6 health)

choices.text: Walk on. Nobody sells a real core in a market

effects.log: A wise rule. Behind you, somebody's rich nephew is counting out eight hundred taels.

events.text: {npc}, the seller of the glass core, finds you at an inn a year later. {He} looks worse: thinner, with a bandaged hand. "I need help," {he} says. "A sect bought one of my cores. Their elder swallowed it. Now they want the beast it came from, and they think I know where it lives. I made it up. But there is a real pool I named in the story. And they are going there."

choices.text: Go to the pool and warn whatever lives there

effects.log: You reach the pool a day before the sect. You feel foolish shouting at water. That night the pool is suddenly half as deep, and the next morning the sect finds only mud and frogs.

choices.text: Turn {npc} over to the sect

effects.log: The sect pays sixty taels and takes {npc} away. They do not go to the pool after all. You tell yourself that is something.

choices.text: Help {npc} disappear

effects.log: A change of clothes, a forged travel pass, a boat south. {npc} grips your hand at the jetty and swears {he} is finished with lies. You do not believe {him}, but you like {him} better for swearing it.

events.text: A letter reaches you from the south, in a hand you know. "I sell fish now," {npc} writes. "Real ones. Last week something huge came up under my boat and pushed it gently into the best fishing water I have ever seen. I think it knew. I think it was saying thank you to you, through me. Come and eat fish."

choices.text: Go south and eat fish

effects.log: You spend a month on a boat with an honest liar, and the fish are excellent, and every evening a ring spreads out across the water from nowhere, as if something had come up to listen.

choices.text: Write back, and keep the letter

effects.log: You keep the letter in the bottom of your pack for the rest of your life. On bad days you take it out and read the line about the fish.

events.text: A sect you are visiting keeps a secret under its main hall: a flooded cistern, and in it a serpent as long as a warship, chained with talisman-written iron through the gills. The elder who shows you down is proud. "Its blood feeds our foundation pills. A cup a month. It does not mind." The serpent opens one eye. It minds.

choices.text: Say nothing, but come back alone at night

effects.log: You memorise the stairs, the guards, the lock. On the way out you pass the pill hall, where the disciples are lining up for their monthly cup and laughing.

choices.text: Ask for a cup of the blood yourself

effects.log: It is cold and bitter and goes into your meridians like sleet. Your qi leaps. That night you dream you are chained in the dark and somebody is laughing upstairs.

choices.text: Tell the elder this is an abomination

effects.log: The elder stops being proud and starts being polite, which is worse. You are escorted to the gate before evening.

events.text: Midnight in the cistern. The talisman chains hum. The serpent lifts its head out of the black water until its eye is level with your lantern and, in a voice like a rockfall a long way off, says: "Thirty years. Cut the third chain and I will do the rest."

choices.text: Cut the third chain

ok.log: The chain parts with a sound like a bell breaking. The serpent does the rest: the cistern wall, the hall above it, a great deal of the sect's roof. It goes down the mountain in a flood of black water to the river. In the confusion nobody sees you leave. Nobody ever proves it was you.

fail.log: The talismans flare and throw you across the cistern. Guards come running. You get out over the wall with a wound and a sect that will want to talk to you for years. (-25 health)

choices.text: Tell it you cannot, and leave

effects.log: "Then you are like the others," it says, "only sadder." It sinks. You hear the words for a long time afterwards.

choices.text: Ask it what it knows, first

effects.log: It tells you, in a cold slow voice, about pools under the earth and the pearl that falls once in a thousand years. You leave before dawn knowing more than the sect's whole library, and having done nothing at all.

events.text: Years after the night of the cistern, the river that runs past that sect's mountain floods its lower halls every single spring, and only its halls, and the villages below have had the best harvests in living memory. The sect has put a price on the head of whoever freed the serpent.

choices.text: Visit the river and say hello

effects.log: You stand on the bank at dusk. A long dark shape passes upstream under the surface, slows beside you, and goes on. That is all. It is enough.

choices.text: Keep your head down and your secret close

effects.log: You never go near the place again. But you smile every spring when you hear the news from the river.

events.text: The new county magistrate wants paddy fields, and the only water in the valley is the old dragon pool. {npc} has hired forty labourers to cut a channel and drain it. The villagers stand at the edge of the work, silent. Not one of them will lift a spade.

choices.text: Go to {npc} and argue for the pool

ok.log: You tell {npc} about the droughts the pool has broken and the floods the old records say followed every time somebody touched it. {npc} is a careful official. {He} decides to dig a well instead, and to take the credit for having thought of it.

fail.log: {npc} hears you out politely and has you shown off the site. The digging goes on.

choices.text: Sabotage the channel by night

ok.log: You fill the channel back in three nights running. The labourers decide the pool is doing it and walk off the job. {npc} cannot hire anybody within twenty miles after that.

fail.log: Caught with a spade at midnight. A night in the cells and a fine of twenty taels, and the channel is finished a week later. (-10 health)

choices.text: Take a spade: the magistrate pays well

effects.log: Fifteen taels for a week of digging. The villagers will not sell you food. The water level drops a hand-span a day.

events.text: The channel is open. The dragon pool is draining into the new fields, lower every day, and on the seventh day the black water at its centre begins to move in a slow circle, all by itself, and the sky over the valley goes the colour of a bruise.

choices.text: Run down and warn the labourers out of the channel

effects.log: You get them out with moments to spare. The pool does not drain; it rises, all at once, a standing wall of black water that goes down the new channel and through the magistrate's new fields and the magistrate's new house. Nobody dies. The pool is fuller than before.

choices.text: Stand at the edge of the pool and try to calm it

ok.log: You sit and breathe with it, the way you would steady a frightened horse. The circling slows. The bruise-coloured sky passes over. The magistrate fills in the channel the next day, very quietly, and has a shrine built on the bank.

fail.log: The water comes up and takes you down the channel with everything else. You wake three miles downstream in a mulberry tree.
fail.deathCause: a dragon pool that did not want to be drained

events.text: The magistrate, {npc}, is retiring, grey now, and has asked to see you. {He} has kept the dragon pool clean for twenty years with {his} own salary. "I wanted to thank somebody," {npc} says. "And everybody else who was there that year is dead."

choices.text: Walk up to the pool together

effects.log: The two of you sit on the bank with a jar of tea. A ring spreads across the water. "Every year," {npc} says. "Every year it does that when I come." {He} seems very happy about it.

choices.text: Accept the thanks and go on your way

effects.log: You bow. {npc} bows. It is enough.

events.text: A storm stands on the far mountains all evening, motionless, like a tower of black cloud. You are on a threshing floor with half the village watching it when the lightning shows a shape inside it: long, impossibly long, rising in coils toward a single point of light at the top of the cloud. An old woman beside you, a baby tied on her back, shades her eyes and says, loudly and clearly: "Look at that. A snake."
events.arc: The Word on the Threshing Floor

choices.text: Shout over her: "A dragon! It is a dragon!"

effects.log: Your voice cracks across the threshing floor. The baby on her back wakes and shrieks with joy, and in the cloud the long shape reaches the light, and closes on it, and goes up, and up, and is gone. The old woman glares at you. You feel as if you have done something enormous, and you have no idea what.

choices.text: Say nothing. You do not know what it is

effects.log: In the cloud the shape reaches for the light, and seems to falter, and falls back into the storm. The rain does not come. The old woman goes home satisfied. Something about it bothers you for the rest of the summer.

choices.text: Agree with her: it is a snake, a big one

effects.log: The shape in the cloud falls. Not fades: falls, like a rope cut. The storm tears itself apart, and for the rest of the year there is no rain in that country, and hail out of clear skies, and people on the far side of the mountains start talking about a burning wind.

events.text: Years later you find the old woman from the threshing floor, very old now, sitting in a doorway. She remembers you. "The storm on the mountains," she says. "I called it a snake. I have been told since what that means. Do you think I made it fall?"
events.arc: The Word on the Threshing Floor

choices.text: Tell her it rose, because somebody else called it a dragon

effects.log: She laughs and laughs. "My grandson," she says. "On my back. He was screaming dragon at the top of his lungs. Do you think it was him?" You say, very seriously, that it was.

choices.text: Tell her the truth: you do not know

effects.log: "Nobody knows anything," she says comfortably. "I am going to call everything a dragon from now on, to be safe. That cat is a dragon. You are a dragon." It is the nicest thing anybody has said to you in a year.

events.text: A little dragon shrine by the road: a stone the height of your knee carved with a coiled serpent, worn smooth by a thousand thumbs, with a cup of rice and a burnt-down stick of incense in front of it.

choices.text: Leave a coin and bow

effects.log: One copper in the cup. On the road that afternoon the rain holds off exactly until you reach the inn.

choices.text: Rest in its shade and meditate

effects.log: There is a cool, slow current in the air around the stone, like the breath of a deep pool. You sit in it for an hour.

choices.text: Walk past

effects.log: You walk past. A crow on the shrine watches you go.

events.text: The roadside dragon shrine you always stop at has been knocked over: the stone serpent lies face down in the ditch, and the cup is smashed. Wheel ruts. A cart, carelessly driven.

choices.text: Set it upright again

ok.log: It takes an hour and a borrowed ox. When it is back on its feet you put a new cup in front of it. On the road for years afterwards, you never once lose your way.

fail.log: You hurt your back and only get it halfway. Three days later you pass again and somebody has finished the job. The new cup has rice in it. (-5 health)

choices.text: Leave it: it is only stone

effects.log: It is only stone. Your horse goes lame within the mile. Probably unrelated.

events.text: On the bed of a dried-up lake you find a monk, {npc}, kneeling in the dust and chanting, very hoarse. "There is a serpent under this lake," {he} tells you, when you give {him} water. "I asked it for rain. It said heaven had not ordered rain, and that if it gave rain without the order, heaven would punish it. I asked it anyway. Should I have?"

choices.text: Say the people come before heaven's paperwork

effects.log: {npc} smiles with cracked lips. "That is what I said too." That night it rains on the dead lake for the first time in two years.

choices.text: Say it was wrong to ask the serpent to suffer for you

effects.log: {npc} bows low. "Then I will ask heaven instead," {he} says, and goes on chanting. It does not rain. {He} does not stop.

events.text: At last the rain comes to the dead lake, and with it a storm that does not stop. Lightning has been striking the lake for three days, over and over, in the same place. {npc} is standing on the shore. "Heaven is punishing it," {he} says. "For my rain. I cannot let it die for me."

choices.text: Help {npc} hide the serpent

ok.log: You and {npc} wade into the lake to your chests and the monk chants a sutra of concealment while you hold a temple bell over your heads like an umbrella. Something cold and long coils round both your legs and stays very still. The lightning hits the water a hundred paces away, and again, further, and then goes off looking somewhere else. Afterwards the old tellers will say this is how heaven was fooled. They will leave you out.

fail.log: A bolt hits the water near enough to throw you both onto the shore. The storm passes at dawn. In the mud of the lake there is a long, shallow, empty trench. Nobody knows if it escaped or died. (-25 health)

choices.text: Tell {npc} that this is between heaven and the serpent

effects.log: {npc} goes in alone. On the third night the lightning stops. {npc} comes out at dawn, half burned and smiling, and will not say a word about it, then or ever.

events.text: An old swordsman by the river has given his whole life to one technique: the Reverse Scale Thrust, an upward stroke meant to find the one scale under a dragon's throat that grows the wrong way. "I have never seen a dragon," he admits. "But if I ever do, I will be ready. Do you want to learn it?"

choices.text: Learn it, seriously

effects.log: A whole autumn of one stroke, upward, over and over, at a drawing pinned to a willow. It is a very good stroke. It has no use against anything that is not a dragon. You are not sure he knows that.

choices.text: Ask him what he would do if a dragon actually came

effects.log: He thinks about it for a long time. "Run," he says at last. "But I would run knowing I could have done it." That, it turns out, is the whole art.

events.text: Years after you learned the Reverse Scale Thrust, a hunting party offers you a fortune to come with them. "We need someone who knows the stroke," their leader says. "There is a Gyo in the lake country. Old. Slow. Full of qi."

choices.text: Refuse: the stroke was never meant to be used

effects.log: You send them away. That night you practise the stroke once, alone, upward, at nothing, and then put it down for good.

choices.text: Go with them

ok.log: The Gyo rises out of the lake like a hill getting up. You find the throat. You find the scale. You do not stop to think. The party pays you a hundred and twenty taels and the murim gives you a nickname you do not like.

fail.log: You find the throat. You find the scale. You touch it. The old stories are right about what happens next.
fail.deathCause: touching the reverse scale of a Gyo

choices.text: Go with them, and warn the Gyo first

effects.log: You get to the lake a day early and shout at it, which feels ridiculous. When the party arrives the lake is empty and the leader looks at you for a long time. You are never hired by hunters again.

events.text: In a lake village you find the people building a little raft hung with red silk. The headman explains without shame: every ten years the lake god takes a bride, and every ten years the lake does not flood. This year's bride is the potter's daughter. She is fourteen and has stopped crying because she is too tired to cry.

choices.text: Say you will speak to the lake god yourself

effects.log: The headman laughs. Then he sees your face. The raft waits for you to come back, and so, in the dark, does the lake.

choices.text: Take the girl and run

ok.log: Over the wall with the girl on your back before anybody can shout. You leave her with an aunt in the next province. Behind you, the lake village waits for its flood. It does not come.

fail.log: The village is faster than you thought and angrier. You are beaten and thrown out on the road. You do not know what happens to the girl. (-12 health)

choices.text: Leave: their gods, their village

effects.log: You leave at dawn. You find that you cannot remember the girl's face, afterwards, and that this is worse than if you could.

events.text: At midnight you row out onto the lake alone. The water parts. A head rises, wide as the boat and pale with age, with whiskers like mooring ropes. "Another one," it says wearily. "Do you know, I have never once asked for a bride? They throw them in, and I carry them out to the far shore and let them go, and nobody believes them when they come home."

choices.text: Ask it to tell the village itself

effects.log: It comes up at dawn in front of the whole village, huge and pale and exasperated, and says one sentence: "No more brides." Then it sinks. The potter's daughter becomes the most famous potter in the province, mostly of serpent jars.

choices.text: Promise to spread the truth yourself

effects.log: It thanks you with a look and goes down. You spend the next week finding the brides of the past forty years, all alive on the far shore, and bringing them home one by one.

events.text: A famous painter in the provincial capital is finishing a dragon on the wall of a temple: forty feet of black ink, every scale perfect. Every scale but the eyes, which are empty. "If I paint the eyes," {npc} says, perfectly seriously, "it will fly away."

choices.text: Dare {npc} to paint the eyes

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long moment. "Come back in a year," {he} says. "I need to finish being afraid first."

choices.text: Ask to learn to paint like that

effects.log: A month grinding ink and painting scales. You never get good. But you learn to see how a thing is put together, which is useful when the thing is somebody's sword form.

choices.text: Laugh at the old story

effects.log: {npc} does not laugh. {He} just adds another scale, very carefully, and goes on not painting the eyes.

events.text: A year later, to the day. The temple is full: word has spread. {npc} climbs the scaffold with a brush loaded with black ink, hands trembling, and dots one eye, and then the other.

choices.text: Watch the dragon

ok.log: There is a sound like a sheet of silk tearing. Thunder in a clear sky. When the dust settles there is a long dragon-shaped space on the temple wall, clean plaster, and a storm going away north. {npc} sits down on the scaffold and laughs until {he} cries.

fail.log: Nothing happens. The crowd groans. Then it rains, gently, inside the temple, from the ceiling, for exactly as long as it takes {npc} to climb back down. Nobody can explain it. The painting stays, eyes and all.

choices.text: Watch {npc}

effects.log: Whatever the wall does, you watch the old painter's face. It is the face of somebody who has been afraid of one thing for forty years and has just, finally, done it. You think about that face often.

events.text: An apothecary is selling dragon bone by the ounce, ground fine for calming the spirit. The bones on the counter are huge, grey, and stone-heavy, with old teeth still in a jaw. You have never seen a dragon. You have also never seen anything like this jaw.

choices.text: Buy an ounce of powder (10 taels)

effects.log: Ten taels. It tastes of chalk. Your spirit is calmer for a month, which could be the bone or could be the ten taels you can no longer spend on anything foolish.

choices.text: Ask where the bones come from

effects.log: A cliff three days west, where the river cut down through the hills and left bones sticking out of the rock like roots. "The old dragons," the apothecary says, "who died before there were people to see them."

choices.text: Walk on

effects.log: Old bones, old stories. You have your own to get on with.

events.text: The dragon-bone cliff, three days west: a red river gorge, and in the rock face, a skull the size of a house, and a spine running away along the cliff for a hundred paces. Diggers are chipping at it with picks.

choices.text: Sit under the skull and meditate

effects.log: Whatever it was, it died a very long time ago and it was not a dragon in any way a storyteller would recognise. But the stone has a stillness to it older than any sect. You come away steadier.

choices.text: Chase the diggers off

ok.log: They go, grumbling, and the province's apothecaries complain for a year about the price of dragon bone.

fail.log: There are more of them than you thought and they are all holding picks. (-8 health)

events.text: On the eastern shore a storyteller tells the children the old one: the Dragon King of the East Sea fell sick, and only a rabbit's liver could cure him, so the turtle went ashore and talked a rabbit into coming down to the palace under the sea. And the rabbit, when it understood, said it had left its liver drying on a rock at home.
events.arc: The Turtle and the Dragon King

choices.text: Ask how the story ends

effects.log: "The turtle carried the rabbit home to fetch it," the storyteller says, "and the rabbit jumped onto the beach and laughed at him all the way up the hill." The children cheer. You think the turtle had a hard life.

choices.text: Ask if the Dragon King got better

effects.log: The storyteller pauses. "Nobody ever asks that," {npc} says. "The old fishermen say the king is still sick, down there. And still sending turtles."

events.text: Late at night on the same beach, by your fire, an enormous old turtle crawls up out of the surf and looks at you with weary, polite eyes. "I do not suppose," it says, "that you are a rabbit."
events.arc: The Turtle and the Dragon King

choices.text: Tell it, regretfully, that you are not

effects.log: "No," it says. "Nobody ever is, these days." It accepts a piece of dried fish, tells you the Dragon King sends his regards to anyone who is kind to his servants, and crawls back into the sea. Your next sea voyage has a following wind the whole way.

choices.text: Offer it medicine for the king

effects.log: You give it the best salve in your pack. It looks at the jar for a long time. "Nobody has ever just given me something," it says. "I will tell him." It goes down into the waves holding the jar very carefully in its mouth.

choices.text: Ask it to take you to the palace under the sea

ok.log: It considers you, and the sea, and then lets you hold onto its shell. What you see down there you will never be able to describe properly. When you come up, three days have passed on the beach, and you feel younger than when you went down.

fail.log: It sighs and dives, and you hold on for a few strokes until your lungs give out. It brings you back up, politely, and leaves you on the sand. (-8 health)

events.text: Off the eastern coast there is a little rocky island where, they say, a king of an old kingdom was buried at his own wish under the sea, so that he could become a dragon and guard the coast forever. The fishermen still bow to it when they pass.

choices.text: Meditate on the shore facing the island

effects.log: The sea breathes in and out through the channel in the rock. After an hour you are breathing with it. After a day you understand, just a little, what kind of promise it would take to choose that.

choices.text: Swim out to it

ok.log: You reach the rock exhausted and sit on it in the spray. Below, in the green water of the channel, something long turns over once, slowly, like a sleeper, and settles again.

fail.log: The current says no. A fishing boat pulls you out and the fishermen tell you, at length, what they think of people who swim to a king's grave. (-10 health)

events.text: Pirates are raiding the eastern coast. The night before they are expected at the fishing village by the king's island, the whole sea around the rock begins to glow faintly green.

choices.text: Stand on the beach with the villagers

ok.log: The pirate ships come in at dawn and never reach the beach: a long swell rises under them out of a flat sea and rolls them over like toys. You and the villagers only have to pull survivors out of the water and tie them up. The old men bow toward the island all morning.

fail.log: Two boats get through. It is an ugly fight on the sand. The rest of the fleet is rolled over by a wave out of a flat sea. You live. (-15 health)

choices.text: Row out to the rock and ask the king for help

effects.log: You kneel on the wet rock in the dark and ask, feeling foolish. Nothing answers. At dawn the pirate ships come in, and the sea gets up under them out of a flat calm and puts every one of them on the reef.

events.text: Hail in midsummer, out of a single black cloud, the size of pigeon eggs: the barley is flattened in an hour. The farmers say there is a Gangcheori in the mountains, a failed serpent that wanted to be a dragon and now hates everything that grows.

choices.text: Help the farmers save what they can

effects.log: You spend three days with your back bent in the mud, propping up stalks, which is harder than any sword training. Half the crop lives. The farmers feed you for a month.

choices.text: Go up the mountain and look for the thing

effects.log: You find scorched trees in a perfect line, and on a cliff a boulder cracked by cold. Whatever it was, it went north. You follow.

events.text: At the top of the northern ridge, in a dry ravine, you find it: a serpent as long as a temple, grey as ash, its scales dull and cracked, curled round a dead tree. It does not look at you. "They called me snake," it says to nobody. "So I am a snake."

choices.text: Tell it you would have called it a dragon

ok.log: It turns its head. For a long time it says nothing. Then it uncoils and goes down the far side of the mountain into the clouds, and the hail stops, and does not come back, and in the spring the farmers say the black cloud has gone somewhere far away to think.

fail.log: "Words," it says, and the hail starts. You get off the mountain bruised from head to foot, knowing more than you did about grief. (-15 health)

choices.text: Fight it, for the farmers

ok.log: It fights like something that does not care if it lives. In the end it does not. The hail stops. The farmers build you a shrine you do not deserve.

fail.log: It is too old and too bitter. You leave the mountain with frost burned into your skin in the shape of scales. (-30 health)

choices.text: Leave it its grief

effects.log: You go back down. The hail goes on, less often. Some things cannot be fought or comforted, only outlived.

events.text: An old scholar, {npc}, is writing the great book of beasts and has heard you have travelled. "Serpents," {he} says. "Everybody tells me about dragons and nobody tells me about the serpents in between. What have you seen?"

choices.text: Tell {npc} everything, carefully and truthfully

effects.log: A whole afternoon. {npc} writes everything down and asks better questions than any master you have had. You find you have seen more than you knew.

choices.text: Exaggerate wildly, for the fun of it

effects.log: You describe a nine-headed river snake that sings. {npc} writes it all down with a perfectly straight face. Fifty years later scholars will still be arguing about the Singing Serpent of your home province.

events.text: A parcel arrives: the finished Book of Serpents, in nine volumes, from {npc}, who has died. Your name is in the preface. A note in a shaky hand says: "Volume seven. The ladder. Read it."

choices.text: Read volume seven

effects.log: The ladder: egg, viper, water snake, great serpent, river serpent, imugi, flood serpent, cloud-seeker, dragon. Each rung with its trial. Reading it, you find yourself thinking about your own cultivation in rungs too, and something stuck in you comes loose.

choices.text: Give the books to a sect library

effects.log: The library puts your name on a little plaque. Within a few years three sects are arguing about volume seven. {npc} would have loved it.

events.text: Halfway across the big river, the boat stops. Not slows: stops, as if it had run onto a sandbank in the middle of deep water. The boatman drops the oar and starts praying. Under the hull, something scaled is sliding past, and it goes on sliding past for much longer than anything should.

choices.text: Sit very still until it has passed

ok.log: It passes. The boat floats free. The boatman will not take your fare, and will not stop shaking.

fail.log: Its tail flicks at the end, almost playfully, and the boat goes over. You swim to shore with your sword in your teeth. (-10 health)

choices.text: Strike down into the water with your sword

ok.log: Your blade bites scale. The river heaves, and the boat is thrown a hundred paces downstream into the reeds. You will never know if it was anger, or just a shrug.

fail.log: The river answers. The boat is gone and so is a good part of you.
fail.deathCause: a river serpent you struck from a boat

choices.text: Drop a little rice into the water as the boatman does

effects.log: A handful of rice from your pack on the water. The sliding stops; the boat lifts very gently and is set down three lengths further on, pointed the right way.

events.text: You dream of a shining bead falling through a black sky, turning over and over, and wake with your hand closed on nothing. For a moment the room smells of rain and cold deep water.

choices.text: Lie still and follow the feeling

effects.log: You breathe slowly until dawn, and the cold-water calm stays with you all morning.

choices.text: Get up and write it down

effects.log: Pearl. Falling. Something reaching. You read it the next day and it is just words. But you keep the page.

events.text: The blind beggar under the bridge says he was a hunter once, and that he lost his eyes to an Imugi. "Looked it in the eye," he says. "The last thing I saw. Gold, as big as a wagon wheel. Worth it." He holds out his bowl.

choices.text: Give him a few coins and listen to the whole story

effects.log: He tells it well: the hunt, the pool, the eye. "It did not hate me," he says at the end. "It was sorry. That is what I cannot forgive."

choices.text: Ask what he would do differently

effects.log: "Bring it a rice cake," he says, at once, as if he had thought about it every day for forty years. "Instead of a hook."

events.text: The blind hunter under the bridge is dying, and has asked for you. "There is a pool," he whispers. "North of the three pines. Take it a rice cake. Tell it a hunter is sorry."

choices.text: Go, with a rice cake

effects.log: You put the rice cake on a stone at the edge of the black pool and say the words. Nothing moves. In the morning the rice cake is gone and in its place, wet and gold-green, is a single scale. You take it back to the bridge. He is gone. You leave it where he used to sit.

choices.text: Promise, and stay with him instead

effects.log: He dies before dawn holding your sleeve. You never quite find the time to go north. You are sorry about that for a long while.

events.text: Fog comes down on the lake so fast and so thick you cannot see the prow of your own boat. Then a voice, low and unhurried, from everywhere in the fog at once: "You have a heavy sword and a light heart. Which of them brought you onto my water?"

choices.text: Answer honestly

effects.log: You tell it why you came. It listens to the whole thing without interrupting. "Better than most," it says, and the fog lifts, and you are at the far shore, which is not where you were rowing.

choices.text: Draw your sword

ok.log: Your blade cuts the fog into two clean halves and nothing else. A low sound like laughter goes through the water. "That answers it," it says, and the fog lifts.

fail.log: Something hits the boat from below and you are in the water, in the fog, with no idea which way is up. You crawl ashore an hour later. (-15 health)

choices.text: Ask it a question back

effects.log: "What are you?" you ask. "Waiting," it says. "Like you. Only longer." The fog lifts.

events.text: The fog comes down on the lake again, years later, as if it had been waiting for you. "I have been thinking about you," the voice says. "A thousand years is long. A conversation is short. Ask me one thing."

choices.text: Ask how to break through your bottleneck

effects.log: "Stop pushing," it says. "Water does not push. It is just heavier than whatever is in its way, for longer." You spend the winter thinking about that. In spring something in you gives.

choices.text: Ask what it is waiting for

effects.log: "A pearl," it says, "and a storm, and a human who will look up and say the right word." A long pause. "I am not asking you. Yet."

choices.text: Ask its name

effects.log: It is quiet for so long that you think it has gone. Then it tells you. It is a long name, and old, and nobody has asked it in four hundred years. You never tell anyone.

events.text: The river has been rising for nine days in Jiangnan, and today the farmers say a Gyo is coming down it: a flood serpent, with the whole river behind it. The dyke above the town is the only thing between ten thousand people and the water.

choices.text: Stand on the dyke and hold it with your qi

ok.log: All night in the rain with your palms on the wet earth, pushing. In the brown water beyond, something enormous turns its head and looks at the little human holding the dyke, and turns aside, and takes the river with it into the empty marshes. The town lives. The children will sing about you.

fail.log: The dyke breaks under your hands.
fail.deathCause: the flood serpent, holding a dyke

choices.text: Organise the evacuation

effects.log: All night in the rain, pulling people out of houses and pointing them up the hill. By dawn the town is on the hills. The dyke goes at noon. The water takes the houses and none of the people. (-6 health)

choices.text: Go upstream and face the Gyo itself

ok.log: You stand on a rock in the middle of the flood and look a Gyo in the eye. You do not fight. You just stand there, refusing to move, and it is so surprised that it goes round you, and round the town, and on.

fail.log: The rock goes, and you with it, a mile downstream. (-25 health)

events.text: A year after the flood, a stranger comes to your door in a cloak that drips, though it has not rained. {He} has gold eyes. "I came to see the human who stood in my way," {npc} says. "You were very small."

choices.text: Invite {npc} in for tea

effects.log: The tea in the pot goes cold the moment {npc} touches the cup, and {he} drinks it with great pleasure. You talk about rivers until dawn. When you open the door to see {him} off, {he} is gone, and so is the puddle.

choices.text: Bow, and say nothing

effects.log: {npc} bows back, a little stiffly, as if {he} were not used to the shape. Then {he} walks away down the road and turns into rain before the corner.

events.text: A guild of beast-core hunters wants you. {npc}, their captain, lays it out plainly over a fire: a Thousand-Year Imugi in a lake two provinces away. Its core would take a sect master to the next realm. They need one more master-level fighter. A tenth share.

choices.text: Accept

effects.log: Fifty taels in advance. {npc} shakes your hand with a grip like a vice. Two weeks to the lake.

choices.text: Refuse

effects.log: {npc} shrugs. "Plenty of others," {he} says. You suspect that is true, and the knowledge sits with you on the road.

choices.text: Accept, intending to sabotage the hunt

effects.log: You take the advance with a smile. {npc} looks at you a beat too long before shaking your hand.

events.text: The lake. The hunters set talisman chains round the shore by night. At dawn {npc} rings a bronze bell over the water, and the lake rises: a head like a hill, eyes like twin moons, and a voice everyone hears in their own skull. "Go home," it says. "All of you. I am very old and very tired, and I do not want to kill anybody today."

choices.text: Fight with the hunters

ok.log: It is a terrible day. When it is over the lake is red and {npc} is holding up a core as bright as a lantern. Your share is a hundred and fifty taels and a flask of the creature's qi. You drink it. It tastes like an apology.

fail.log: It did not want to kill anybody. It does.
fail.deathCause: a Thousand-Year Imugi that asked you to go home

choices.text: Turn on the hunters and break the talisman chains

ok.log: You cut the chains at three posts before {npc} sees what you are doing. The lake does the rest, gently, washing the hunters and their gear up onto the bank in a heap. When you look back, the great head is watching you, and it inclines, very slightly.

fail.log: You cut one chain before the hunters are on you. In the confusion the beast gets away. So, barely, do you. The guild will remember your face. (-25 health)

choices.text: Lower your sword and go home, as it asked

effects.log: You turn your back on the lake and walk. Behind you {npc} curses you. Behind you, a little later, the hunt goes very badly, and you are not there for it.

events.text: The Martial Alliance has called a council: a Gyo in the western lakes has been seen calling rain without heaven's leave, and the sects are divided. Some want it hunted for its core; some want a pact with it; some want it left alone. They want to hear from experienced masters. They want to hear from you.

choices.text: Argue for a pact: protect it, and it protects the region

ok.log: You speak for an hour. When you sit down the hall is quiet, and then the Wudang elder stands and bows. The vote goes your way by two.

fail.log: You speak well, and lose by a vote. The council decides to "observe" the Gyo, which means nobody knows what will happen.

choices.text: Argue for the hunt: a beast that rains without leave is a danger

effects.log: The hunting sects cheer. The vote goes your way. You are asked to lead the first party, as a mark of honour.

choices.text: Argue that it is none of the Alliance's business

effects.log: "The weather," you say, "was here before us, and will be after." Several old masters laugh. The council adjourns without a vote, which, in the Alliance, is a victory of sorts.

events.text: The pact with the Gyo of the western lakes has held for years. Now there is a drought on the plain, and the Alliance asks you, as the pact's author, to go and ask the Gyo for rain. It would be rain without heaven's leave. The Gyo would be punished for it.

choices.text: Ask it, and stand with it when heaven answers

ok.log: It rains on the plain for three days. On the fourth, heaven's lightning comes for the Gyo, and you stand in the lake beside it and put your qi against the storm. Both of you live. Neither of you says much afterwards. Neither of you needs to.

fail.log: It rains. Heaven answers. You are thrown out of the lake burned to the bone. The Gyo lives. It sends a fish to your sickbed every day for a month. (-30 health)

choices.text: Refuse: the pact does not mean it bleeds for us

effects.log: The Alliance is annoyed. The Gyo, when you tell it, is quiet for a long time. Then it sends a little rain anyway, a careful thin rain that heaven might not notice. Heaven does not.

events.text: You lead the Alliance's hunting party to the western lakes. The Gyo is waiting for you, coiled on the surface in broad daylight. "I have been calling rain for two hundred years," it says, "for farmers your Alliance has never heard of. Go ahead, then."

choices.text: Fight

ok.log: You win. The Alliance hangs a scale in its great hall. Two summers later the farmers by the western lakes have their first drought in two hundred years, and somebody writes your name on a wall there, with a word after it.

fail.log: It wins.
fail.deathCause: the Gyo of the western lakes, at the Alliance's order

choices.text: Call off the hunt in front of your party

effects.log: You sheathe your sword. Half the party never speaks to you again. The Gyo watches you go and, that summer, the western lakes have the best rains in memory.

events.text: You visit a small mountain sect that nobody in the murim dares attack, and see why: a serpent as thick as a watchtower coiled round the base of the gate, asleep in the sun. The disciples step over its tail on their way to practice. "The pact is three hundred years old," the gatekeeper says. "It guards us. We keep its pool clean and tell it the news."

choices.text: Ask to be the one who tells it the news today

effects.log: You sit by its great head and tell it about the world below: the sects, the wars, a scandal in the Namgung family. Its eye opens a slit when you get to the scandal. You make the scandal longer.

choices.text: Ask the sect how such a pact is made

effects.log: "Badly, at first," the gatekeeper says. "Our founder fed it for years before it trusted him. It is not a contract. It is a friendship that got old."

choices.text: Ask whether it is ever unhappy

effects.log: The gatekeeper thinks about it. "In spring," {npc} says, "it looks up at the storms for a long time. We do not ask about that."

events.text: News: an alliance of three sects has marched on the little mountain sect with the guardian serpent, carrying binding talismans. They do not want the sect. They want the serpent.

choices.text: Go and stand at the gate with them

ok.log: Three days at the gate. On the third, the serpent wakes fully for the first time in a century, and the besiegers discover what three hundred years of friendship looks like when it is angry. You are given the right to step over its tail forever.

fail.log: You are wounded on the first day. The serpent carries you up to the sect hall in its mouth, very gently, and then goes back down to finish things. (-28 health)

choices.text: Go to the besiegers' camp and talk them out of it

ok.log: You ask them, one by one, what they will say to their own disciples about how they got the core. One by one they find reasons to go home.

fail.log: They hear you out and march anyway. You hear afterwards that the siege went very badly for them.

choices.text: Stay out of it

effects.log: You stay out of it. A month later you hear that the besiegers went home in pieces and that the serpent asked, specifically, whether you had been there.

events.text: A village child, {npc}, has been seen meditating every dawn by the waterfall pool, and the village says a snake is teaching {him}. You watch from the trees. A silver serpent as long as a boat lies in the shallows, and every time the child's breathing goes wrong, it hisses, softly, and the child corrects.

choices.text: Leave them alone

effects.log: You watch for a week and learn more about breathing than in your first ten years. Then you leave them to it.

choices.text: Offer to teach {npc} swordwork, to go with the breathing

effects.log: The serpent watches you very carefully the first day. On the second it goes to sleep. You take that as permission.

choices.text: Take {npc} away to a proper sect

effects.log: The child cries all the way to the sect gate. That night the river floods the sect's lower terraces. They send the child home in the morning.

events.text: {npc}, the child the serpent taught, is grown, and has just won the Gathering of Young Heroes with a breathing method nobody has ever seen. {He} finds you in the crowd afterwards. "It sent me to say thank you," {npc} says. "For leaving us alone. Or for the sword. It said you would know which."

choices.text: Ask {npc} to show you the breathing

effects.log: {npc} shows you, there in the noise of the arena. Slow. Heavy. Like water deciding to move. Your own qi settles deeper than it has in years.

choices.text: Ask whether the serpent is well

effects.log: "It is old," {npc} says. "It says it is close to something. A storm. It wants me to be there to watch." {He} looks at you. "You too, I think."

events.text: On a bare hill you find a grave with a strange headstone: a fang, curved and yellow-white, taller than you are. Carved into it: HERE LIES A HUNTER WHO WON. Below, smaller, in a different hand: AND WAS SORRY.

choices.text: Pay your respects

effects.log: You bow to the hunter and, after a moment, to the fang. The wind goes over the grass in long waves, like something swimming.

choices.text: Dig at the foot of the fang

ok.log: A wrapped bundle: a hunting journal, and a sliver of scale that still holds a cold, slow power. The journal ends: "If anyone reads this, do not hunt the old ones. They are only trying to go home."

fail.log: Only earth and stones, and a very bad feeling you carry for the rest of the month. (-6 health)

events.text: You pass the grave with the fang headstone years later. Somebody has been tending it: the grass cut, a fresh cup of clear water at the foot of the fang. The prints in the mud around it are not a person's. They are long and wide and smooth, like something heavy dragged along the ground.

choices.text: Wait by the grave for whoever comes

effects.log: At dusk a serpent as long as a village street comes up the hill out of the mist, pushes the cup of water a little straighter with its nose, and goes away again without looking at you. You do not understand it at all. You understand it completely.

choices.text: Leave your own cup of water and go

effects.log: Two cups now, side by side at the foot of the fang. It feels right.

events.text: A voice in your sleep that you have not heard before, and yet you know it: low, old, wet as a riverbed. "Great one of the humans. In nine days I rise. The first human to see me will speak a word, and the word will decide what I become. I would rather it were you."

choices.text: Promise to be there

effects.log: "A mountain three days north," it says. "The one with the split peak. Be early. They are always early." You do not ask who.

choices.text: Ask why you

effects.log: "Because you have walked far enough on your own road," it says, "to know that a word is a kind of strength. Most humans think words are wind."

events.text: The split peak, the ninth night. The storm comes in from three directions at once. Out of the valley below rises a serpent long enough to wrap the mountain, four claws spread, and at the top of the storm a pearl hangs like a small moon. Then the claws close on it. And then, on the ridge opposite, you see them: a band of cultivators, core hunters, who have come early, and their leader is drawing breath to shout.

choices.text: Shout first: "DRAGON!"

effects.log: Your voice, with all your qi behind it, goes round the mountains like a gong. The serpent shivers from head to tail. Horns break out of its brow like branches in spring, and it goes up, and up, and the storm goes with it, and the rain that falls on the valley afterwards tastes of something sweet. The hunters on the far ridge never get their word out.

choices.text: Silence the hunters before they can speak

ok.log: You cross the gap between the ridges in two breaths and put the leader on the ground with a hand over the mouth. In the silence a child in the valley, woken by the storm, yells "dragon!" in a thin high voice, and that is enough. It rises.

fail.log: You are too slow. The word they shout is "snake". The serpent falls back into the storm like a rope cut, and the mountain shakes, and for a year there is no rain in that country. (-25 health)

choices.text: Say nothing: it is not your word to say

effects.log: You hold your breath. The hunters shout "snake!", and it falters, and then from somewhere far below, in a village, a baby on somebody's back starts screaming the only word it knows. The serpent hears it. Nobody ever finds out which baby.

events.text: A rival master you defeated years ago sends you a gift: a water gourd. Inside, coiled in the dark water, is a tiny serpent with gold eyes. The note says: "Found in a drained pool. It will not eat. I am told you know about these things."

choices.text: Carry it into the mountains to a deep pool

effects.log: A week on foot to a pool deep enough. You tip the gourd into the black water and the little serpent hangs there a moment, looking up at you, then dives. You feel absurdly as if you have done something important.

choices.text: Keep it, and find out what it eats

ok.log: It eats moonlight on water, it turns out. You leave the gourd open on the windowsill on clear nights, and it grows a finger a year, and you talk to it more than to most people.

fail.log: It will not eat anything. In a month, desperate, you take it to the river after all. It is very thin. You hope it is not too late.

events.text: The serpent you have kept in a gourd on your windowsill for years is too big for it now: it lies along the whole windowsill like a silver belt, and on stormy nights it presses its nose to the shutter and stares.

choices.text: Take it to the big lake at last

effects.log: It hesitates on the shore, the way children do at a school gate. Then it goes. On your birthday every year after that a fish appears on the lake shore by your favourite rock, laid out neatly, head pointing to your house.

choices.text: Keep it a little longer

effects.log: One night in a thunderstorm the shutter is open in the morning and the windowsill is empty. You are not angry. You are a little hurt. You leave the shutter open for a year.

events.text: In a river gorge two Imugi are fighting: one white as bone, one black as a burnt beam, each the length of a warship, locked together in the churning water. Above them, very high, a single pearl of light hangs in the clouds. There is only one.
events.arc: The Two Serpents in the Gorge

choices.text: Watch, and learn

effects.log: All day. The way they wind and unwind is a martial form older than any sect, and by dusk you have a dozen ideas about footwork that will keep you busy for years. Neither wins. The pearl drifts away.

choices.text: Shout at them that there might be room for two

effects.log: Two enormous heads turn up toward the tiny human on the cliff. For a long moment they stare. Then they go back to fighting, but more slowly, and when you leave they are lying side by side in the shallows, breathing hard, looking at the sky.

choices.text: Back the white one with a thrown blade

ok.log: Your blade bites the black one's flank. It turns, sees you, and in that breath the white one pins it. The black one sinks away, bleeding. You are not sure you did anything good.

fail.log: The black one's tail sweeps the cliff top. You are thrown into the trees. (-20 health)

events.text: A great storm stands over the gorge where you once shouted at two fighting serpents. In the lightning you see them: white and black, wound round each other like two threads in a rope, rising together toward one pearl.
events.arc: The Two Serpents in the Gorge

choices.text: Call out "dragons", plural

effects.log: They rise together, and the pearl takes them both. For a breath, at the top of the storm, there are two shapes with horns, and then one shape, and then sky. The rain that falls is warm.

choices.text: Watch in silence

effects.log: Whether they made it, you cannot say. But they went up together, and you were the one who suggested it, and that will have to be enough.

events.text: The night of the river lanterns. A thousand little paper lights on the water, each with a prayer. And among them, quietly, as if it had every right to be there, a pale serpent head as wide as a door rises, and looks at the lights, and does not do anything else at all.

choices.text: Float your lantern straight to it

effects.log: Your lantern bumps gently against its jaw. It looks at the writing for a long time. Then it nudges the lantern back into the current, very carefully, and sinks.

choices.text: Keep the children calm

effects.log: "It is only looking," you tell them. "It likes the lights." They believe you so completely that, for the rest of their lives, they will tell their own children the same thing.

choices.text: Draw your sword and wade in

effects.log: It sinks the moment you move. Two hundred people turn and look at you, standing waist-deep in a festival river with a drawn sword. You go home by a back street.

events.text: At your level, heaven's officials sometimes speak to you directly. One appears in your courtyard tonight, a clerk of the Ministry of Rain, with a scroll. "A serpent in your province has been raining without orders," {npc} says. "Heaven requests your assistance in its punishment."

choices.text: Refuse heaven

effects.log: {npc} blinks. "Nobody refuses," {he} says. "Somebody just did," you say. {npc} writes that down, carefully, and goes away. You have a feeling there will be paperwork.

choices.text: Argue the serpent's case

ok.log: You list the harvests saved, the villages fed. {npc} listens, sighs, and rolls up the scroll. "A warning, then," {he} says. "Tell it to file a request next time."

fail.log: {npc} listens politely, says the law is the law, and goes to find somebody else. You hear thunder in the hills that night.

choices.text: Assist, as heaven asks

effects.log: You hold the serpent while the lightning comes. It does not fight you. It only looks at you. The ministry sends a polite letter of thanks, which you burn.

events.text: The Ministry of Rain has been thinking about your refusal. The clerk, {npc}, is back with a different scroll. "We have a proposal," {he} says. "Somebody to stand between heaven and the serpents of this world. To judge which rains are worth a little rule-breaking. Unpaid. Permanent."

choices.text: Accept

effects.log: You sign. From then on, in dry years, the serpents of three provinces come to you at night, very politely, to ask whether they may. You almost always say yes.

choices.text: Decline politely

effects.log: "Very well," {npc} says. "But you will be asked again in your next life." {He} seems to mean it.

events.text: Walking a mountain ridge for an hour, you realise the ridge is breathing. Trees grow on it; moss, rocks, a little shrine somebody built two hundred years ago. Far ahead an eye the size of a pond opens, gold under grey lids. "You are heavy," it says. "Heavier than most. Sit, and let us be heavy together."

choices.text: Sit with it for a season

effects.log: Autumn, winter, spring. Neither of you says much. When you stand up, you find that a sapling has started to grow in the crook of your elbow, and that your qi has the slow, deep weight of a mountain.
