choices.text: Ask why it never tried for the pearl

effects.log: "I tried four times," it says. "Four times they called me a snake. After the fourth I decided I liked being a mountain." It closes its eye. "It is not so bad. People build shrines on you."

events.text: News from the mountains: the breathing ridge has moved. Overnight, the whole thing, trees and shrine and all, has shifted three miles east and lifted its head toward a storm. Villagers are fleeing.

choices.text: Go and stand by it as it tries a fifth time

effects.log: You reach it as the storm breaks. It says: "Say it." And you say it. Somewhere in the lightning, a forest takes to the sky.

choices.text: Help the villagers instead

effects.log: You spend the night carrying the old and the sick down the valley. By dawn the ridge is gone, and a new river runs where it lay. Nobody ever tells you whether it rose. The river is very clear.

events.text: You have been walking for three days across a white mountain range above the clouds of the Upper Realm when you notice that the mountains are warm, and scaled, and very slowly rising and falling.
events.arc: The Mountain That Sleeps in the Sky

choices.text: Keep walking, very quietly

ok.log: You reach the end of the range, which is a tail, and step off onto ordinary cloud. Behind you the mountains sigh and turn over in their sleep. You have walked the length of a sky dragon and it never noticed. You decide never to tell anybody, and tell everybody.

fail.log: A scale shifts under your foot and you slide a mile down its flank into a cloud bank. It does not wake. You are very glad. (-15 health)

choices.text: Sit down and meditate on its back

effects.log: The breath of a dragon is a long, long thing. Matching it takes you a year. When you finally do, the Upper Realm's qi goes into you like water into sand.

choices.text: Knock politely

effects.log: You rap on a scale with your knuckles. An eye the size of a lake opens on the horizon. "Hm," it says. "A walker." The eye closes again. "Come back when I am awake."

events.text: The sky dragon is awake. It has come looking for you, which in the Upper Realm means a sudden shadow over half a province and every immortal looking up. Its head comes down through the cloud until its eye is level with yours.
events.arc: The Mountain That Sleeps in the Sky

choices.text: Ask it what the world below looked like when it left

effects.log: "Smaller," it says. "Wetter. There was a pool. A child used to bring me rice cakes." It is quiet for a while. "Is there still rice, down there?" You tell it yes. It seems pleased.

choices.text: Ask it to carry you to the edge of the sky

effects.log: You ride behind its horns for a day and a night to the place where the Upper Realm thins into stars. At the edge you see the worlds below laid out like lanterns on a river, and somewhere among them, very small, the one you came from.

choices.text: Challenge it to a duel, for the honour

ok.log: It accepts with what looks like delight. You do not win. You do not lose. It is the best fight of your existence, and afterwards it calls you "small cousin" and means it kindly.

fail.log: It flicks you, not unkindly, across three provinces. (-30 health)

events.text: Far out beyond the last cloud of the Upper Realm, where heaven turns into night, something flies: a dragon with wings. Not a sky dragon. Older. An Eungryong, the last form of all, of which there may be three in all the heavens. It is coming your way.
events.arc: The Mountain That Sleeps in the Sky

choices.text: Bow low

effects.log: It passes over you so close you feel the wind of its wings in your bones. It does not stop. But in passing, it looks down, and its look says: I was a snake in a pool once. Remember that.

choices.text: Fly up alongside it

ok.log: For one long moment you fly wingtip to fingertip with the last of all dragons. Then it climbs into the dark where you cannot follow. It is enough. It is more than enough.

fail.log: The wind of its passing alone throws you tumbling down through the cloud layers for a day. (-20 health)

events.text: The Upper Realm's Bureau of Rains is a hall a mile long with ten thousand desks. Outside, waiting in a queue that stretches out of sight, are dragons: true dragons, horned and clawed, each holding a numbered tile in its mouth, waiting for a warrant to rain on a world below. The clerk at the nearest desk, {npc}, looks at you hopefully. "Are you the new temporary assistant?"

choices.text: Say yes, for the experience

effects.log: A year of stamping rain warrants. You learn the name of every dragon in the queue, and that most of them were imugi in little pools somewhere, once, and that every one of them remembers who called them a dragon.

choices.text: Help a dragon at the back of the queue jump to the front

ok.log: Its world below is in a drought. You talk {npc} into an emergency stamp. The dragon takes the warrant in its teeth and dives through the floor of heaven. Far below, a village you will never see gets its harvest.

fail.log: There is a form for queue-jumping. It takes eleven years. The dragon thanks you for trying.

events.text: {npc} from the Bureau of Rains hurries up to you with a sealed scroll. "An imugi in the world below," {he} says. "It caught its pearl tonight. The witness has not spoken yet. The Bureau needs an observer from up here. You are from down there, are you not?"

choices.text: Go down and watch the ascension

effects.log: You stand invisible above a storm over a little country you do not know, and watch a serpent rise toward you holding a pearl. Far below, a grandmother opens a toothless mouth. You hold your breath. The word is "dragon", said grudgingly, and it comes up past you, horns breaking out of its brow, and looks at you as it passes, and you think: so that is what it looks like from up here.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to send somebody else: you would interfere

effects.log: {npc} nods. "That is why we asked you," {he} says. "The ones who know they would interfere are the only ones who do not." {He} sends somebody else. The serpent rises.

events.text: In a back courtyard of a heavenly palace a long grey serpent with no horns is sweeping up fallen jade petals with a broom held in its tail. It notices you watching. "I fell," it says, without being asked. "A thousand years ago. The witness said snake. But I fell upward, a little, by accident. So now I sweep."

choices.text: Pick up a broom and help

effects.log: You sweep together until dusk. It tells you about its pool, which was in a country you have heard of, and about the old woman who said "snake". "She was right," it says, "at the time."

choices.text: Ask if it is unhappy

effects.log: "I was, for the first five hundred years," it says. "Then I noticed that the petals were beautiful." It goes on sweeping.

events.text: The grey serpent who sweeps the heavenly courtyard comes to find you, broom still in its tail. "There is a storm in the Upper Realm tonight," it says, "and a pearl in it. I am not young. I would like to try again. Will you watch, and say the word?"

choices.text: Watch, and say "dragon"

effects.log: It rises through the heavenly storm, grey and old and stubborn, and closes its claws on the pearl, and you say the word. Horns. Light. The broom falls past you, spinning, and you catch it. You keep it forever.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let heaven decide

effects.log: It rises, and catches the pearl, and nobody speaks, and it hangs there for a long time between snake and dragon. Then it comes down again, slowly, and picks up its broom. "Well," it says. "At least nobody said snake." It seems happier than before.

events.text: You have never been to this pool before. But when you kneel to drink, a ring spreads across it from the middle, and a fish jumps out onto the stone at your knee, and another, and another, as if somebody below were very glad to see you and did not know how else to say it.

choices.text: Thank the water

effects.log: You say thank you to a pool. It does not feel foolish at all. Something in another life helped something in this water, and the water has a long memory.

choices.text: Put the fish back

effects.log: One by one, back into the pool. A low sound comes up from the deep, like laughter heard through a wall.

events.text: Every pool you pass this year goes still when you come near. Not a frog croaks. Not a fish rises. At the third one an old fisherman looks at you and shifts his boat further off. "The water does not like you," he says. "What did you do?" You have no idea. Some part of you does.

choices.text: Go to the deepest pool and kneel by it

effects.log: You kneel by the black water until dark without knowing what you are apologising for. In the morning, very faintly, a frog croaks.

choices.text: Shrug it off

effects.log: Water is water. And yet the dreams that year are full of a pool with nothing in it.

events.text: A storm sits on a mountain far away all night, and you stand at the window watching it, and you cannot shake the feeling that you were supposed to be there, once, in a life you do not remember, and that you walked away.

choices.text: Go to the mountain

effects.log: By the time you get there the storm is gone and the pool at the top is clear and still. On the bank, in the shape of somebody sitting, the stone is worn smooth. You sit. It fits.

choices.text: Stay at the window until dawn

effects.log: You watch until the storm breaks up. This time, at least, you watched to the end. It feels like it counts.

events.text: At the back of a night market a merchant unwraps a sword for you alone: a blade made of overlapping scales, green-black, each one fitted to the next as if it had grown there. It hums when you are near it. It has never hummed for anyone, the merchant says, and narrows {his} eyes. "Four hundred taels. Or perhaps it is yours already, and you only need to say so."

choices.text: Buy it (400 taels)

effects.log: Four hundred taels. The hilt fits your hand as if your hand had been made for it, which, in a way, it was. On rainy nights the blade is cold and wet though it has been in its sheath.

choices.text: Lay your palm on the blade and wait

ok.log: The scales ripple under your hand like a living thing settling. The merchant goes white, wraps the sword, and pushes it into your arms. "Take it," {npc} says. "It was never mine. It was waiting."

fail.log: For a moment the blade goes cold as deep water, and you see, very clearly, a pool, and hooks, and a sky full of hunters. Then the merchant wraps it up again and you are just a customer who cannot afford it.

choices.text: Walk away. Some things should not be carried twice

effects.log: You walk away. Behind you the sword hums once, low, like something being let go of.

events.text: A tournament. Your opponent's sword shatters on the scale blade. Then the next. Then a famous master's. In the evening a grey old hunter comes to your inn. "My grandfather made that sword," he says, "from the Imugi he killed. He told me on his deathbed it should go back to the water. He never had the courage. Do you?"

choices.text: Take the sword to the deep pool and give it back

effects.log: You stand at the edge of a black pool and drop it in. It does not sink like iron. It swims, once round, and goes down. That night it rains for the first time in that valley in a generation. You have never felt so light.

choices.text: Keep it: it chose you

effects.log: The hunter bows and goes. The sword stays at your side for the rest of your life. You never lose a fight in the rain.

choices.text: Give it to the hunter to decide

effects.log: He holds it for a long time, weeping, and then walks out into the night toward the mountains. You never find out what he did with it. You suspect you know.

events.text: A museum of the Martial Alliance, a hall of famous weapons. In a case in the corner, labelled only The Sword of Scales, a blade of green-black scales lies on silk. As you pass it, the glass fogs from the inside.

choices.text: Put your hand on the glass

effects.log: The fog draws itself into a shape on the inside of the glass, briefly: a coil, and an eye. Then it clears. The curator rushes over. You say you did not touch anything, which is almost true.

choices.text: Ask the curator its story

effects.log: "Scales of an Imugi killed by hunters, oh, very long ago," the curator says. "It is said it never quite forgave them. It is also said that it is not, strictly speaking, dead." The curator laughs. You do not.

events.text: In the courtyard of an old mountain temple a round stone is set into the ground, wider than a cart, carved with talismans and a coiled serpent. It is cracked. Through the cracks comes a faint cold breath. "The seal," the old monk sweeping beside it says. "A great serpent, sealed below by our first abbot. Lately it has been talking in the night. It keeps asking for someone." {npc} looks at you strangely. "It describes someone like you."

choices.text: Lie down on the stone and listen

effects.log: Under the stone, far down, something breathes, and in the breath there are words in a voice like your own heard through deep water. It knows your name. You do not know how it knows your name.

choices.text: Help {npc} repair the cracks

effects.log: A week of mortar and talisman paper. When the last crack is closed, the breathing stops, and you feel a sadness you cannot account for.

choices.text: Leave this temple quickly

effects.log: You leave before dark. That night, three valleys away, you dream of being under a stone and hearing somebody walk away overhead.

events.text: You come back to the temple of the seal. It is midnight. The cracks in the stone are glowing green. Under it, something is saying, in a voice you now know is a little like yours: "I was you. Or you were me. Either way, you have the hands, and I have the waiting. Break it."

choices.text: Break the seal

ok.log: The stone splits with a sound like a mountain clearing its throat. Out of the dark below comes a serpent the colour of old jade, uncoiling and uncoiling, and it rises past you into the night and is gone toward the nearest storm. As it passes it touches your forehead with its nose, very lightly, the way you might touch your own reflection.

fail.log: The talismans hold, and throw you across the courtyard. Under the stone the breathing sighs and settles back to waiting. (-25 health)

choices.text: Strengthen the seal: the monks had their reasons

effects.log: You put your qi into the talismans until they burn white. The voice under the stone goes quiet. "Fair," it says, at last. "I was not a very good serpent, either." You sit by the stone until dawn.

choices.text: Talk to it through the stone until dawn

effects.log: It tells you what it remembers of a long life in deep water and the monks who came with bells. You tell it about your life. At dawn neither of you has decided anything, and both of you feel less alone.

events.text: Since the night you broke the seal, the rains in that mountain country have been gentle and exactly on time. The temple's monks are furious. The farmers have built a new shrine, and on it, crudely carved, is a figure that looks a great deal like you.

choices.text: Visit the shrine

effects.log: There is rice in the cup in front of your carved face, and the carving has been rubbed smooth on the nose for luck. You bow to yourself. It is very strange. It is not unpleasant.

choices.text: Visit the monks and apologise

effects.log: The new abbot hears you out, then sighs. "Our founder wrote that the seal would be broken by the one it was made against," the abbot says. "We did not understand. Go in peace, serpent."

events.text: The province is burning. No rain for two years, and hail out of clear skies, and a hot wind that smells of lightning. The farmers have a name for what is doing it: Gangcheori, the failed one. When you hear the name, your chest goes tight, as if somebody had said something terrible about you.

choices.text: Go up into the burnt mountains to find it

effects.log: You go north. The trees get blacker and the stones get hotter. At night you dream of a storm, and a pearl, and a voice from below saying one word that was wrong.

choices.text: Stay and dig wells with the farmers

effects.log: Three wells in a season. One of them strikes water. A village lives through the summer because of it, and the old women put your name in their prayers, next to a name they will not say.

choices.text: Leave the province

effects.log: You leave. The hot wind follows you to the border, and stops there, as if it had been seeing you off.

events.text: On the burnt summit, coiled round a dead pine, lies the Gangcheori: grey, cracked, huge, smoking faintly like a kiln. It lifts its head and looks at you, and something in its ruined face changes. "You," it says. "I know you. You were the one who was not called dragon." A long pause. "Or I was. It is hard to tell, at this distance."

choices.text: Call it a dragon. Now, too late, and mean it

ok.log: You say the word. It shudders all along its length. Nothing grows; no horns break out. But the smoke stops. And that night, for the first time in two years, it rains on the province, a thin, ashamed, beautiful rain.

fail.log: "Too late," it says, and the hail comes down. But it lets you climb down alive, and you think that might be something. (-20 health)

choices.text: End it, for the farmers

ok.log: It does not fight very hard. At the end it lays its head on the burnt earth and says: "Thank you." The rain comes within a day. You do not feel like a hero at all.

fail.log: It has nothing left but spite, and spite is very strong.
fail.deathCause: the Gangcheori, in the burnt mountains

choices.text: Sit with it, and do nothing at all

effects.log: You sit by it for three days in the heat. On the third it says, "Nobody has sat with me before." On the fourth, the hail stops. That is all. It is not nothing.

events.text: Years after you sat with the drought dragon, the burnt province is green again. On its old mountain there is a new pool, very deep and very clear, and the farmers say that on summer evenings something grey lies in it looking up at the clouds, not trying for anything, just looking.

choices.text: Go and look at the clouds with it

effects.log: You lie on the bank and it lies in the water and neither of you speaks. A cloud shaped like a pearl goes over. It does not reach for it. You think it might, one day.

choices.text: Leave it its peace

effects.log: You do not go. Some things heal better unwatched.

events.text: You walk into the great shrine of the Azure Dragon of the East with a crowd of pilgrims. Every stick of incense in the hall bends its smoke toward you at once, like grass in a wind. The pilgrims fall silent. The old priest drops his ladle.

choices.text: Bow to the dragon on the wall

effects.log: You bow. For a breath, the painted dragon's eye seems to look back with something like recognition, and a great deal of amusement. Outside, a light warm rain begins from a clear sky.

choices.text: Back out of the shrine

effects.log: You back out, very fast, apologising to the incense. The priest follows you down the steps and presses a blue scale into your hand without a word.

events.text: The priest of the Azure Dragon shrine sends for you. "The dragon has asked," he says, "through the oracle sticks, through the incense, through a fish that jumped onto the altar, for the human whom the smoke bowed to. It says: guard the east for a while, as it once did. It will owe you a favour."

choices.text: Guard the eastern coast for a year

effects.log: A year of pirates, sea-raiders and one very angry sea monster. The coast holds. On the last night, the sea lights up blue for a mile, all along the shore, and you understand that you have been thanked by yourself.

choices.text: Ask the dragon, through the priest, who it was

effects.log: The oracle sticks fall in a pattern the priest has never seen. He reads it slowly. "It says: a pool, a child with a rice cake, a thousand years, and a word. It says you would not remember. It says that is all right."

events.text: You are a guest of a family that has been lucky for three hundred years: never a fire, never a flood, never a son who gambled the land away. In their storehouse, among the rice, lies a black serpent as thick as a tree. When you come in with a lamp, it lifts its head and looks at you, and does not look away.
events.arc: The House That Was Always Lucky

choices.text: Look back at it

effects.log: For a long moment you look at each other, and you have the strangest feeling of being home. The family's grandmother watches from the door. "It never looks at guests," she says. "Who are you?"

choices.text: Bow, as the family does

effects.log: You bow. It inclines its great head. The family exchange looks and give you the best room in the house.

events.text: A message from the lucky family: their youngest son has fallen in with gamblers and is threatening to sell the storehouse, serpent and all, to a sect that wants its core. "It looked at you," the grandmother writes. "It has never looked at anyone. Come."
events.arc: The House That Was Always Lucky

choices.text: Go and talk the son round

ok.log: You take the son to the storehouse at night and make him look the serpent in the eye. He comes out an hour later white and silent and burns the gambling notes himself.

fail.log: He will not listen. But when the sect men come with carts, the storehouse is empty. The serpent has gone. Within a year the family has lost everything, and the son is the first to say why.

choices.text: Pay the son's gambling debts (150 taels)

effects.log: A hundred and fifty taels. The son weeps. The serpent sleeps on in the rice. The family will be lucky for another three hundred years, and on its genealogy scroll, in a margin, they add your name.

choices.text: Carry the serpent away to a safe pool yourself

effects.log: It lets you lead it out by night to a deep pool in the hills. It goes in, then turns and looks at you for a long time. You understand that it is not going back to that house, and that it chose you instead. You never have a fire, or a flood.

events.text: A small lakeside sect teaches something nobody else in the murim does: the Breathing of the Deep. Its founder, they say, was a fisher's child taught at the edge of this lake by a great serpent who gave up the sky to do it. When you try the first form, the elder stops talking and stares. You are doing it exactly right, and nobody has shown you.

choices.text: Ask to study here

effects.log: A season in the lake to your waist at dawn, breathing slow and heavy as water. Your qi settles deeper than it ever has. The elder keeps watching you, and once, quietly, asks whether you were ever a fish.

choices.text: Ask about the founder's teacher

effects.log: There is a stele on the shore with a coiled serpent cut into it. "It never said its name," the elder says. "It said it had been a snake and nearly a dragon, and that it had decided teaching was more interesting than either." You stand in front of the stele for a long time.

events.text: The lakeside sect's elder is dying and has called you to the shore. "The founder left a last form," the elder says, "that nobody has ever been able to do. The founder's teacher said: the one who can do it will be the one who taught it, come back. Try."

choices.text: Try the last form

ok.log: You breathe in until you are as heavy as a lake, and out until you are as light as mist, and the whole lake breathes with you, once, a long slow swell from shore to shore. The elder laughs, and cries, and dies happy before evening. The sect asks you to stay. You do, for a while.

fail.log: Close. Very close. The lake shivers but does not breathe. "Next time," the elder says, and means it in a way you do not quite like, and dies before evening.

choices.text: Decline: the form should go to a disciple of theirs

effects.log: You point out a quiet young disciple who has been watching from the reeds. The elder smiles. "That is exactly what the teacher would have said," the elder says.

events.text: The old well in the village square has a stone lid nobody is allowed to lift: the Dragon Well, the grown-ups call it, and they will not say why. Tonight the other children have dared you to look in.

choices.text: Lift the lid and look

ok.log: Far, far down, past the moss and the cold, two gold lights open in the black water, look up at you, and close again. You put the lid back very gently. You never tell the others what you saw. They never stop asking.

fail.log: The lid is too heavy. It slips and crushes your fingers. The grown-ups find you, and you learn the rule about the Dragon Well again, at length. (-4 health)

choices.text: Refuse: rules are rules

effects.log: They call you a coward for a week. That autumn, when the river fails, the Dragon Well is the only water in the village, and the old men lift the lid with a bow.

choices.text: Drop a pebble down instead

effects.log: The pebble falls for a long time. Then, a long time after it should have hit the water, it comes flying back up out of the well and hits you on the forehead.

events.text: Grown and back in the village, you find a drought, and the old men arguing at the Dragon Well: lift the lid and draw from it, or leave it shut, as the rule says?

choices.text: Tell them what you saw down there as a child

effects.log: They listen in silence. Then they lift the lid together, bow, lower one bucket, and draw it up full and cold and sweet. The well never runs dry that summer. Nobody draws more than one bucket a family.

choices.text: Draw the water yourself, quickly and without ceremony

effects.log: The water is bitter, and the next morning the well is dry, and the gold lights in the dark are gone. The old men look at you for a long time.

events.text: The dragon boat races on the river: twenty long boats with carved heads, drummers pounding, the banks packed. You are paddling for the town. Halfway down the course, your boat suddenly surges ahead as if pushed, and under the green water you see a long dark shape keeping pace just below your hull.

choices.text: Paddle harder and say nothing

effects.log: You win by four lengths. The town carries your crew round the square. You do not mention the shape. Under the bridge that night, you leave a zongzi on the water.

choices.text: Stop paddling: it is not a fair race

effects.log: Your crew stares at you. The boat slows; the shape sinks away. You lose by a length. On the bank, an old woman who saw it all nods at you, approving, which is better than a prize.

choices.text: Shout to the crowd that a real dragon is racing

effects.log: Nobody believes you. Everyone laughs. Next year, though, the race committee quietly adds a twenty-first lane, and leaves it empty.

events.text: Every year since the race you paddled, the twenty-first lane on the river has stayed empty. This year a child asks you, loudly, in front of the whole race committee, who the empty lane is for.

choices.text: Tell the child the truth

effects.log: You tell it simply: something long and dark that once pushed your boat to a win. The child nods as if this were obvious. That afternoon, in the empty lane, the water ripples all the way down the course, a breath ahead of the leading boat.

choices.text: Say it is for the boats that sank long ago

effects.log: A good answer, and partly true. The committee looks relieved. The child does not look convinced.

events.text: A cheap manual from a market stall: The Coiling Serpent Fist, "learned by watching an Imugi in its pool for thirty years." Most of it is nonsense. One page is not: a diagram of how a serpent turns its whole body into a single coil before it strikes.

choices.text: Practise that one page until it is yours

effects.log: A whole winter of spiralling on a riverbank stone. By spring you can put the force of your heels into the tips of your fingers. Your sparring partners are not happy about it.

choices.text: Go and watch a real snake instead

effects.log: A water snake in the shallows, every morning for a month. The manual was half right. The other half you learn from the snake.

events.text: A sparring match against {npc}, a proud sect disciple who has never lost. On the third exchange your body remembers the riverbank: you coil, all of you, from heel to fingertip.

choices.text: Strike with the full coil

ok.log: {npc} goes backwards off the platform and into the crowd. In the stunned quiet somebody says "snake style" and it sticks. You do not mind.

fail.log: You uncoil a breath too soon and {npc} steps inside it. You lose, but you know exactly why, which is worth more. (-10 health)

choices.text: Hold it back: a sparring match is not a fight

effects.log: You let the coil go without striking and lose on points. Afterwards {npc} finds you. "What was that?" {npc} asks. "Teach me." You become friends.

events.text: Deep in the Upper Realm there is an orchard of silver trees where pearls grow like fruit, each one glowing, each one a Yeouiju. The gardener, {npc}, explains: when one is ripe it falls through the clouds into a storm in a world below, and somewhere an imugi reaches for it. "Most miss," {npc} says. "It is not my job to aim."

choices.text: Ask to help in the orchard

effects.log: A year of pruning silver branches. You learn that pearls ripen slowly, that they hum when they are nearly ready, and that {npc} talks to every one of them before it falls.

choices.text: Pick a ripe pearl for yourself

ok.log: It comes away in your hand, warm and humming. You hold it for a moment and understand exactly why a serpent would wait a thousand years for this. Then you put it back on the branch. {npc} pretends not to see.

fail.log: The branch whips back and the pearl burns your fingers like a coal. {npc} sighs and binds your hand. "They are not for us," {he} says. (-12 health)

events.text: A pearl is ripe in the heavenly orchard, humming. {npc} the gardener is away. Far below, through a gap in the clouds, you can see a storm over a small mountain, and in the storm, tiny, a serpent rearing out of a black pool, and somewhere, perhaps, a human on a ridge watching.

choices.text: Let it fall where it will

effects.log: It drops, and you watch it all the way down, and you do not see whether the serpent catches it. When {npc} comes back you say nothing. {He} looks at the empty branch and at your face and smiles.

choices.text: Nudge it, very slightly, toward the serpent

effects.log: A breath on the stem as it falls. Far below, jaws close on light, and the storm goes white. When {npc} comes back {he} looks at the empty branch for a long time. "It is not my job to aim," {he} says. "I did not say it was not yours."
